sources.title: Tom Rhys Harries is ready to take centre stage
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Michael Rudling (Square Mile)
sources.locator: ADHD section ('Finding solace in the complex...' through 'fear was a big driving factor for me'); motorbike section; Parade's End anecdote; opening scene-setting paragraphs
sources.excerpt: “I’ve always had that focus with acting because it’s scary. The impulse to distraction is quietened by the fear of being criticised. I think I was aware from quite a young age that fear was a big driving factor for me.”
sources.context: Long-form in-person lifestyle profile at a Soho members' club ahead of The Seagull's June 2022 return. Also contains: 'I was quite disruptive growing up... often that energy came out in having fights'; 'really strong, protective and nurturing women in my life... There’s one teacher who I’m still in contact with now. I wouldn’t have finished school without her'; 'I’m shit at focusing on something if I’m not interested in it. Then if I am interested in something, I get obsessed with it, because it’s kind of a relief to be able to focus'; motorbikes as 'an antidote... there’s nothing subjective about whether an engine works'; the Parade's End story ('I don’t know who the fuck I thought I was, but I went up to the director...'); the writer's observations that he is 'a man rarely in a rush', that his 'curiosity and openess to the new is palpable', and that he is 'unshy about dropping huge names... He catches my eye to note my reaction.' His most self-disclosing interview found. Single interviewer; writer's framing ('salvation came via the kindness of others') is the outlet's, not his. Writer's opening (verified 2026-11-03): 'The first thing you notice about Tom Rhys Harries is how relaxed he is... this is a man rarely in a rush.' The ADHD statement is in the writer's narration ('He lives with ADHD, a condition that was occasionally tricky in his school days'; 'Rhys Harries’ ADHD has bled into his approach to acting'); the standfirst says he 'talks motorbikes, acting and ADHD'. None of his quoted sentences names the condition. Parade's End story continues: 'Benedict popped up with the book and said he’d had the same concern as me, but that he’d checked the book and it was right... He’s so studious in his work.' Also notes he was about to play Trigorin opposite Emilia Clarke’s Nina in The Seagull at the Harold Pinter Theatre.

sources.title: Tom Rhys Harries and Kit Connor on Fear and Vanity in Hollywood
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries in conversation with Kit Connor (Interview Magazine)
sources.locator: Transcript exchanges on watching himself, preparation ('I really prepare, which has been a crutch'), Clayface prep ('Am I the best judge of myself?'), Elden Ring and anxiety, fear and being needed, Tom Holland, vanity
sources.excerpt: “I really prepare, which has been a crutch. I just shot an indie I loved, and I was like, “This character will benefit from me going in a bit blind,” which was terrifying. I’m so used to having that crutch to lean on.”
sources.context: Peer-to-peer published transcript (print layout leaves hyphenation artifacts such as 'screen test ing' and 'peo ple'; quotes here remove only those line-break splits). Also: 'Am I the best judge of myself? Are you, Kit, the best judge of you?... It’s like an exercise in trying to trust your instinct all the time, isn’t it?'; 'I played Elden Ring to switch my brain off during the three months I was screen testing for Clayface... It probably talks to my level of anxiety throughout that period.'; 'I think fear is a mark of caring about something and wanting to contribute to the greater piece. One of the things I loved most about doing Clayface was how much I’m needed. I felt like I was part of the crew.'; 'the longer I’m allowed to do this, the more it seems to be an exercise in letting go and engaging with people you’re willing to take a leap of faith with'; 'You just hope the editor’s got your back, don’t you?'; 'I may have taken the license to be silly and run with it' (after Connor: 'You taught me how to misbehave on a film set'); 'the vanity of it never interested me. I find it interesting because I feel like I have a relationship to it.'; 'I’m in Los Angeles a lot because my girlfriend’s in L.A.' Friendly peer setting lowers press guard somewhat but it is still a pre-release promotional feature.

sources.title: Tom Rhys Harries Plays a Different Type of Antihero in ‘Clayface,’ DC Universe’s New Horror Hit
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Cultured Magazine (Zoom)
sources.locator: Q&A: 'How are you feeling a couple days out...'; ACL question; bathtub/mask answer; 'Was there a moment in the past 15 years...'; parents at LA premiere; intro paragraphs
sources.excerpt: “I don’t know how to do anything else. [Laughs] I’m really not joking. You commit yourself down a path, and I’ve had way more noes than I’ve had yeses.” ... “I know this sounds trite, but luck plays a huge part in anybody’s perceived success, and the whole thing isn’t a meritocracy.” ... “Ultimately, I just want to be a good, reliable work partner, a good boyfriend, a good brother, son, friend.”
sources.context: Published on release day (2026-10-23) during a multi-city press run; the Q&A itself was conducted 'a couple days out' from release, per the interviewer's question. Also: 'I went through a phase of being nervous... I’ve gone past the point of nervousness. Now I’m just like, “Hey, that’s the film. I hope you like it.”'; ACL: 'I tore it before I started filming... Then I booked Clayface, and I was like, Well, I’m not gonna have time to do the surgery.'; offered to hold his breath 'for like three minutes' in a sealed mask before insurers refused; 'this little voice in my head is like, You are a 35-year-old man. What are you contributing to society?'; watching his parents at the LA premiere was 'one of the most special things to me from this whole experience.' Writer notes he is '36-year-old', 'How much Harries wants this is not in question', and calls him 'clear-eyed and methodical'. Verified 2026-11-03 via plain curl: 'I went through a phase of being nervous... I’ve gone past the point of nervousness. Now I’m just like, “Hey, that’s the film. I hope you like it.”'; on the ACL, 'So there was no time for me to do it. But I’ve put it back in since.'; the writer: 'he is clear-eyed and methodical about the potential for imminent creative fulfillment' and 'he seems to handle the pressure with aplomb.'

sources.title: 5 minutes with: Tom Rhys Harries – 'Strindberg is a headache, but a good one'
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries (WhatsOnStage first-person Q&A)
sources.locator: Paragraphs beginning 'I played loads of Rugby growing up', 'The acting world was so alien to me', 'When I was in third year I auditioned quite a bit in London'
sources.excerpt: “When I was in third year I auditioned quite a bit in London, but obviously I was based in Cardiff, so I spent thousands of pounds on transport. I used to really beat myself up if I wasn’t able to go to one.”
sources.context: Earliest substantial first-person source, from a theatre trade outlet before any screen fame (Creditors at the Young Vic). Also: 'I’m from a very musical family in Cardiff in Wales; my dad was in a band, my mum used to be a writer'; on Hunky Dory: 'I think my naivety held me in good stead as I didn’t really think much of it. But I got cast in that and luckily we were shooting in the summer so I didn’t miss any college'; 'I didn’t feel like I wanted to leave Wales.' Edited as a monologue, so question wording is not shown.

sources.title: SPOTLIGHT: Mr Tom Rhys Harries
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Taj Hayer (The Rakish Gent)
sources.locator: Answers to 'Have you been surprised by its success', 'How like him are you?', 'How awkward are sex scenes?', 'What drew you to an acting career?', 'How do you switch off'
sources.excerpt: “Well I chose to be an actor which on the surface seems to be a pretty reckless choice of career. Both of my parents are teachers and I grew up in a great and safe family environment, but I’ve been self sufficient since I was 17. In some ways we are similar. With optimism, I will always make decisions that I feel might come off.”
sources.context: Phone interview during the first COVID lockdown, after White Lines hit number one on Netflix in 25 countries (per the outlet). Also: 'if you surround yourself with people that you really believe in and that have a good creative vision, then generally those things tend to turn out really well. I had real faith in Alex Pina'; on intimacy scenes, 'all I wanted was to make sure that the other actor was comfortable. I would find myself so occupied with that, that there wasn’t really a chance to get uncomfortable myself'; 'I don’t tend to have my year planned out in advance'; 'Generally I find that acting is like therapy for me where, through someone else’s words, I can process my own experiences'; 'Someone saw me playing guitar in pubs in Cardiff... Without really giving it much thought I wandered into an audition and got in.' Outlet gives his age as 27.

sources.title: The Star Of Netflix Hit White Lines On Making A Stand, Playing A Sociopath And “That Tooth”
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Lili Göksenin (Mr Porter, The Journal)
sources.locator: Opening paragraphs ('I’m not a celebrity'; Black Lives Matter discussion, '15 of our allotted 45 minutes'); tooth paragraph ('No! She’s misquoted me')
sources.excerpt: “No! She’s misquoted me,” he insists. “I was doing a gag.” ... “It was just me not reading the room. But no, I didn’t pull my tooth out. The dental bill would have been so expensive!”
sources.context: Zoom interview opened via the Wayback Machine raw copy (web.archive.org/web/2020id_/...) because the live page returns a stub. Writer reports he insisted 'I’m not a celebrity' and spent about 15 of 45 minutes on George Floyd and Black Lives Matter: 'If I’m granted any kind of platform with the work that I do... it would be completely remiss of me to not speak about it'. Directly corrects the WalesOnline tooth quote (S07). Outlet gives his age as 27.

sources.title: White Lines' Welsh star Tom Rhys Harries on filming Netflix's Ibiza drama
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Kathryn Williams (WalesOnline)
sources.locator: Tooth-scene paragraph; Hunky Dory/education paragraphs; criticism ('looked like a frog') paragraph
sources.excerpt: Asked how it was done, Tom, 28, says: "I actually pulled it out! It’s real, that whole scene is real. I haven’t told anyone that."
sources.context: Home-town outlet interview. He later called the tooth line a gag that was misquoted (S06). Also: 'But I still really wanted to pursue my education... The space that college provides to make mistakes'; on criticism, 'Someone messaged me the other day to say I looked like a frog... To be honest, I do look a bit froggy but I could not care less'; from Pontcanna, Cardiff; parents still live there. Gives his age as 28, which conflicts with a 1990 birth year.

sources.title: 'A whodunit on acid!' Netflix's new star Tom Rhys Harries on his addictive show, White Lines
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Josh Smith (Glamour UK)
sources.locator: Intro quote ('I don’t wobble easily'); Q&A 'How have you managed that idea of turbulence', 'rejection to acceptance', 'piece of advice'
sources.excerpt: “You just have to take stuff on the chin. I have a very thick skin. I have countless more rejections than acceptances, but I choose to do this, so you have to accept that is part of that.” ... “I really hold onto, ‘what is meant for you, won’t pass you by.’ I am not religious in particular, but I do believe that everything happens for a reason and that gives me some kind of peace.”
sources.context: Release-day Zoom Q&A. Also: 'I have been doing this since 2012, so I have gotten to know myself as an actor and as a person. I don’t think I wobble easily. Wait, that’s a terrible quote!'; on lockdown, 'A lot of my tools, coping mechanisms and how I stay on top of my mental health have been taking away from me. So, I have been thinking about how I can adapt, I exercise a lot, I write music'. Writer quotes him saying the chat 'turns into a therapy session'.

sources.title: Meet The Star Of 'White Lines', The Hedonistic Netflix Hit That's Become The Ultimate Lockdown Escape
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Naomi Pike (Miss Vogue / British Vogue)
sources.locator: Paragraphs on portraying drug abuse ('I’d feel a responsibility as an actor'), Axel's masks, Paul Mescal fame question, closing quote
sources.excerpt: “But I’m just trying to keep on top of friends… as soon as I start thinking about me too much it just becomes really boring. I really miss people, but it [the lockdown] has made me feel really fortunate that I get to do what I do — as long as people still want to employ me.”
sources.context: Zoom interview while moving house in lockdown. Asked whether he could rival Paul Mescal's overnight fame: '“I hope not,” he laughed.' On drug storylines: 'particularly on a big platform [like Netflix], I’d feel a responsibility as an actor… in being progressive in how the story is told.' Describes Axel as wearing 'different masks on all the time'.

sources.title: Tom Rhys Harries Readies for ‘Suspicion’
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Kristen Tauer (WWD)
sources.locator: Paragraphs on Welsh-language upbringing, music ambitions, Seagull hiatus
sources.excerpt: The 29-year-old actor is a first-language Welsh speaker, and was raised in a family “steeped in Welsh culture” and music. “I always thought I would go into music and then I kind of stumbled into acting,” he says. Harries enrolled in the Royal Welsh College of Music and Drama, but soon left after he was cast in the film “Hunky Dory” with Minnie Driver.
sources.context: Trade fashion-press profile. The 'soon left' clause conflicts with his own accounts (S04, S07) and Wikipedia's 2012 graduation (S24); treat it as a WWD error. Also: 'Ultimately, I’d love to release some stuff, but I’ve been kicking that barrel down the lane for forever'; The Seagull 'shut down after five performances at the start of the pandemic'; reports he struggled with long COVID. Age given as 29 in February 2022 conflicts with an October 1990 birth date (would be 31).

sources.title: Schön! Interview - Tom Rhys Harries
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries (written answers to Schön! Magazine)
sources.locator: Written answers on playlists/paper round, stage prep, ambitions (Steppenwolf, clowning), closing John Baldessari quote
sources.excerpt: “This is a John Baldessari quote: A) Talent is cheap, B) You have to be possessed, which you can’t will, C) Be at the right place at the right time. Try as you might, so much of this game is out of your hands. Best you can do is get on the train.”
sources.context: Emailed responses (written, therefore more composed than speech). Also: 'When I was younger I’d go around Cardiff listening to film soundtracks and pretend I was in a Truman Show-type situation. I found that made my paper round less mundane'; 'I love the rehearsal time we get when preparing a play and having the space to fuck up, try things that might not work and root a character’s foundations'; prep 'can be anything — I tend to use music, find art, source excerpts... and doodle all over my rehearsal scripts'; 'I’d also like to go study clowning at Le Coq in Paris at some point.'

sources.title: Fred Perry Subculture: Tom Rhys Harries
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries (Fred Perry Subculture questionnaire and playlist notes)
sources.date: unknown (undated page; text references White Lines' 15 May 2020 release, so circa May 2020)
sources.locator: 'Describe your style in three words?'; 'What’s the best gig you’ve ever been to?'; playlist note on 'Harvest'
sources.excerpt: Describe your style in three words? Loose, Hurried, Functional. ... I pretended I knew what she was talking about, agreed enthusiastically and subsequently spent the entire week trying to learn all of their songs. I obviously didn’t do enough studying because she turned to me during ‘I Bet You Look Good On The Dancefloor’ and she was singing along word for word, I crumbled
sources.context: Brand questionnaire, light comic register. The Arctic Monkeys 2006 anecdote (a teenage girlfriend, a cram week, an air-guitar beer spill, a break-up) is told for laughs. Also: bought a Vespa with his first paycheque and rode at 3am with Neil Young's Harvest; was 'a skater when I was a teenager but not a particularly good one'.

sources.title: Tom Rhys Harries on Cartier, acting and his upbringing
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Gentleman's Journal (phone)
sources.locator: Paragraphs on the Cartier Queen's Cup polo, the Cahaya Studio suit, 'looking behind the curtain'
sources.excerpt: “I’m really keen on looking behind the curtain, whether that’s at the madness of the very British polo as a humble Welsh guy, or the amazing way in which my suit was created. I love to engage with people on different shit and this sort of opportunity opens those doors.”
sources.context: Brand-hosted event write-up (Cartier guest). Also: 'This is so far removed from anything I've been to before, and especially my upbringing'; 'I like to be selective about what I go to, as I think you can dilute the fun of it all'; 'My relationship with fashion had been merely functional, and I always just needed to have enough pockets and be comfortable.' Notes he lived in Peckham after a brief countryside stint. Commercial context limits weight.

sources.title: Tom Rhys Harries Reveals ‘Clayface’ Is a Twisted Body Horror Tragedy
sources.speaker: Instinct Magazine, relaying Tom Rhys Harries' Entertainment Weekly cover-story quotes
sources.locator: Sections 'Tom Rhys Harries literally limped through the movie' and 'Tom Rhys Harries may have found his breakout moment'

sources.context: Secondary relay of the EW cover story (S17, not opened). Also relays: 'I had to say to the stunt coordinator, “That action is the worst thing you could do to bust it up.” But we got away with it!' and 'I think most of Comic-Con would go, “Who?!”'. The 'hadn’t told... anyone' line sits awkwardly with having told the stunt coordinator about one action; the full EW text would resolve the sequence. His own S03 account confirms he tore the ACL before filming and postponed surgery.

sources.title: James Watkins says he "auditioned the hell out of" Tom Rhys Harries for Clayface
sources.speaker: Jarrod Jones (The A.V. Club), relaying James Watkins and Tom Rhys Harries quotes to The Hollywood Reporter
sources.locator: First two body paragraphs

I did two fairly long screen tests with James,” Harries told THR. “But I’m untested in this space, so I was glad he did it with me, really, because it meant that we’d had time to workshop the thing before he got onto set.”

sources.title: 'Clayface' Director James Watkins on Why He “Auditioned the Hell” Out of Star Tom Rhys Harries

sources.date: 2026-10-16 (premiere remarks from the 2026-10-13 Hollywood Legion Theater world premiere)

Club relay (S18) for exact wording.

sources.title: Max Minghella Says Clayface Would Have Fallen Apart Without Tom Rhys Harries
sources.speaker: January Nelson (Creepy Catalog), relaying Max Minghella
sources.locator: Body paragraphs 1-9
sources.excerpt: “Tom Rhys Harries on Clayface, I learned so much from him. Just incredibly disciplined, amazing leadership on set,” Minghella said. ... Harries called Minghella the day Minghella landed his Clayface role, then kept in touch throughout production to make sure he felt included.
sources.context: Only named co-star testimony with behavioral detail found, but relayed by a secondary site that does not name the original interview venue and misstates Harries' age as 34 (he is 36). Also reports Minghella said Harries 'never complained' and would FaceTime his family while in prosthetic makeup; quotes: 'He gave it his all, and it was a lot that they asked of him' and 'the responsibility of being a number one on a call sheet.' Premiere-season praise from a co-star; promotional incentive is obvious.

sources.title: Tom Rhys Harries breaks down how he created the unexpected club scene in ‘Clayface’
sources.speaker: The Express Tribune, relaying Tom Rhys Harries in a Metro Entertainment TikTok clip
sources.locator: Body paragraphs 2-5
sources.excerpt: “That was not in the script. That was Rift,” Harries explained, adding that the production team extended filming by a day to accommodate the sequence. The actor said he initially expected Watkins to reject his suggestion when he proposed trying something spontaneous on set.
sources.context: Secondary write-up of a short video clip; 'Rift' is likely a transcription of 'riffed'. The paraphrase that he 'expected Watkins to reject' the idea is the outlet's, not a direct quote. Watch the Metro clip before quoting.

sources.title: ”Clayface”-stjärnan spelade ”Elden Ring” för att överleva auditions
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries (with Naomi Ackie), interviewed by MovieZine; published in Swedish translation
sources.locator: Q&A answer to the audition-process question
sources.excerpt: Tom: Ganska lång och plågsam, faktiskt. Jag försökte tänka på annat genom att spela ”Elden Ring” på min lediga tid mellan provfilmningarna. Det hjälpte mig att koppla bort allt.
sources.context: Junket interview translated into Swedish by the outlet. English sense: 'Quite long and agonizing, actually. I tried to think about other things by playing Elden Ring in my free time between screen tests. It helped me switch everything off.' sources.title: 'Clayface' Breakout Star Tom Rhys Harries on Surviving a Multi-Day Screen Test
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Seija Rankin (The Hollywood Reporter)
sources.locator: Article body, paragraphs 1-2 (screen test, agent), 4 (risk to studio), 5 (support circle), 6 (after opening weekend), 7 (teacher)
sources.excerpt: “I actually cut off my agent and said, ‘Do not tell me who else it is,’” says Harries. “I just needed to be in the zone, without thinking about who they’re considering.” ... “That’s why I’m grateful for the film being received well, because you realize how many people have invested their time and work into this thing.” ... “I haven’t got any grand aspirations of how I’m going to do this now, because fundamentally nothing is going to change — it might open a few more doors in terms of who I’m able to talk to, but otherwise I just want to be involved with projects from creators who I back fundamentally.”
sources.context: First post-release long interview found (six days after the US opening). Also: after the first test he asked for the competitors' names because “by then it would no longer affect me negatively because I was done”; called back for a second test, “I had to put my blinders on”; saw himself as a studio risk: “there are so many moments where an unknown quality could falter... they haven’t got a great reference point as to what I’d be like with the crew, the rest of the cast, and in the press”; found leading a big production “counterintuitive, but it’s actually easier when you have so many people around you”; former teachers FaceTimed him after seeing the film: “when I was in school, I think it was very much a case of, ‘if this kid doesn’t find something to focus on, he’s fucked’... If this teacher wasn’t there, I would not be having this conversation with you right now.” Writer gives his age as 'Now 36' and dates the Mojo West End debut to 2014. Opened via plain curl, 2026-11-03. Full post-release quote verified 2026-11-03: 'fundamentally nothing is going to change — it might open a few more doors in terms of who I’m able to talk to, but otherwise I just want to be involved with projects from creators who I back fundamentally.'

sources.title: 'Clayface' Director James Watkins on the Tragic Ending, Joker Easter Eggs and His Star's Secret Injury
sources.speaker: James Watkins, interviewed by Brian Davids (The Hollywood Reporter)
sources.locator: Intro paragraphs 7-9 and Q&A answers on the car stunt (paragraphs 36-38 of extracted body)
sources.excerpt: There’s a moment in the film when Matt gets hit by a car, and that’s when it came out. Tom had a quiet word with the stunt man about it. ... He still did the jump and the fall, but he was frank about it. We were like, “Yeah, we obviously don’t want to create a lifelong injury for you.” So we had to finesse how we did the stunt ... I thought Tom was absolutely the right actor for the role. ... But it’s not like he was cast to play Premier League or NFL football. He’s acting, so [having foreknowledge of his injury] wouldn’t have made any difference to me.
sources.context: Director testimony, post-opening. Reporter's framing: Harries 'was quietly concealing a significant knee injury to avoid jeopardizing a career-altering role'; 'Watkins and his team remained unaware of the Welsh actor’s torn ACL until Rhys Harries came clean while filming a sequence in which Matt flees a movie premiere and gets hit by a car.' Also reports a $46.5 million global opening, 75% critics / 94% audience Rotten Tomatoes and an A- CinemaScore. Watkins adds Harries texted him a Jimmy Kimmel Live! screenshot tagged 'very meta'. Promo-cycle testimony from the director who cast him, not an independent intimate. Re-opened via plain curl 2026-11-03: the 'Premier League or NFL football... wouldn’t have made any difference to me' answer appears both in the intro paragraph and in the Q&A, directly after 'we had to finesse how we did the stunt'. Watkins's aside that 'some of these film medicals don’t go that deep' is not used.

sources.title: The Empire Film Podcast, The Interviews (ft. Tom Rhys Harries, Taika Waititi, Peyton Elizabeth Lee & Jacob Tremblay)
sources.speaker: Tom Rhys Harries, interviewed by Chris Hewitt (Empire) over Zoom
sources.locator: Episode audio (publisher mp3 via goloudnow page), 00:02:20-00:03:20 (golf/beard banter), 00:03:46-00:04:50 (ACL), 00:07:21-00:07:35 (on set every day); transcribed locally with whisper-cli small.en, ACL passage confirmed in two passes
sources.excerpt: And I'd torn it probably about six months before starting to shoot [Clayface]. And for fear of losing this job, I didn't tell anybody. And then at one point I was shooting a sort of stunt sequence where a car drives into the side of my leg ... And I had to take the stunt coordinator, Jimmy, to the side. And I was like, Jimmy, I'm so sorry, man. I actually don't have an ACL.
sources.context: Unscripted audio, the 'long-form unguarded speech' task from the previous run. Opens with Harries turning the interview on the host (asks about his golf handicap; 'I have my sources, Chris'; 'I don't know. I rarely know what's going on.'). Later: 'throughout this whole shoot, I was never not on set. I was there every single day'; 'you can go full tilt and not burn out'; he and Watkins 'were in lockstep'. Machine transcript, so treat exact punctuation and filler as approximate; the ACL sentence matched across two independent whisper passes. Local transcript kept outside the repo (/tmp/trh-research/audio/) per the no-full-transcripts rule.

sources.title: Welsh star records huge movie success with blockbuster Clayface
sources.speaker: Nation.Cymru staff (relaying Variety)
sources.locator: Paragraphs 7-8 (Variety box-office relay) and 12 (age, Welsh speaker)
sources.excerpt: Clayface nearly just made up its entire $44 million budget with a $43 million haul this weekend at the global box office ... It’s a massive break for the 35-year-old Welsh speaker from Cardiff
sources.context: Welsh national outlet, secondary. Useful for the Welsh-language angle (also notes the Welsh-language film Effi o Blaenau) and as a dated box-office relay. Its age '35' on 2026-10-27 conflicts with an 8 October 1990 birth date and with THR's 'Now 36' (S26), another reason to print the birth year only.

claims.claim: Harries says fear of criticism is what quiets his ADHD-driven pull toward distraction and that he knew from a young age fear was 'a big driving factor' for him.
claims.passage: The impulse to distraction is quietened by the fear of being criticised.
claims.inference: He names fear itself, not ambition or enjoyment, as the engine of his focus. That is the Six's signature: anxiety converted into vigilance and effort.
claims.alternative: A Three could also be driven by fear of criticism (image), and many actors say nerves help them. The quote is one 2022 interview; ADHD is his own framing for the distraction side.

claims.claim: In 2026 he called heavy preparation 'a crutch' he is 'so used to... lean on' and said going into a 2026 indie role 'a bit blind' was 'terrifying'.
claims.passage: I really prepare, which has been a crutch.
claims.inference: Preparation functions as security; removing it produces fear, not excitement. This is the clearest discriminator against Seven, who typically experiences improvisation and the unplanned as freedom.
claims.alternative: Thorough prep is a trained-actor norm (RWCMD, stage background); S11 also shows him loving rehearsal 'space to fuck up', which is play inside a safe container rather than proof of anxiety.

claims.claim: During roughly two to three months of Clayface screen tests he played Elden Ring 'to switch my brain off'. When Connor remarked that it was a tough game to switch off to, he answered that 'It probably talks to my level of anxiety throughout that period' (in S02 'It' refers to choosing such a demanding game; the article separates the two lines with Connor's interjection rather than joining them). He was out cycling 'trying to distract myself' when the casting call came.
claims.passage: It probably talks to my level of anxiety throughout that period.
claims.inference: He openly names anxiety under high stakes and manages it rather than reframing it as fun, consistent across three outlets.
claims.alternative: Distraction-as-coping also reads as the Seven's move away from discomfort; S14 says 'about a two month period' while S02 says three months of screen tests, so the duration varies by account.

claims.claim: Across 2020 and 2026 he describes success as choosing collaborators he believes in: 'I had real faith in Alex Pina' (2020); acting is 'an exercise in letting go and engaging with people you’re willing to take a leap of faith with' and 'You just hope the editor’s got your back' (2026).
claims.passage: You just hope the editor’s got your back, don’t you?
claims.inference: Security is located in trusted people and their backing, a Six pattern that holds six years apart in different contexts.
claims.alternative: Trusting the director and editor is professional common sense for any actor who does not control the final cut; a Nine would also emphasize letting go.

claims.claim: He glosses fear as 'a mark of caring about something and wanting to contribute to the greater piece', says what he loved most about Clayface was 'how much I’m needed. I felt like I was part of the crew', and says his goal is to be 'a good, reliable work partner, a good boyfriend, a good brother, son, friend.'
claims.passage: One of the things I loved most about doing Clayface was how much I’m needed. I felt like I was part of the crew.
claims.inference: Belonging, reliability and duty to the group are the values he volunteers when asked about meaning, which supports Six (loyalty, being a dependable member) over Three (distinction) or Seven (experience).
claims.alternative: 'How much I’m needed' could indicate Two; being 'number one on the call sheet' creates real duties regardless of type; these lines arrive in release-week press where gratitude and team talk are expected.

claims.claim: Co-star Max Minghella, as relayed by Creepy Catalog, called Harries 'incredibly disciplined' with 'amazing leadership on set'; the site's own narration (not a Minghella quote) says Harries phoned Minghella the day Minghella was cast and kept in touch to make sure he felt included.
claims.passage: Just incredibly disciplined, amazing leadership on set
claims.inference: Behavioral testimony that matches C06: he looks after group cohesion and reliability, not just his own performance.
claims.alternative: Premiere-season co-star praise; relayed by a secondary site that misstates his age and does not name the original venue. Inclusive outreach also fits Two or Nine.

claims.claim: In a 2015 WhatsOnStage piece, recalling his third year at drama school (about 2011-12), he said he auditioned in London from Cardiff, 'spent thousands of pounds on transport' and 'used to really beat myself up' if he could not make an audition. The source contains no fear language.
claims.passage: I used to really beat myself up if I wasn’t able to go to one.
claims.inference: Shows early self-reproach over missed chances. Reading it as vigilance is the author's inference; cost and ambition explain it equally, so it is not counted as fear-as-driver evidence.
claims.alternative: Self-criticism is also typical of One and Three; striving drama students commonly do this.

claims.claim: He describes himself as 'quite disruptive growing up', not malicious but with energy that 'often... came out in having fights', and credits 'strong, protective and nurturing women', including a teacher he is still in contact with and without whom he 'wouldn’t have finished school'. In October 2026 he said his schooldays were 'very much a case of, ‘if this kid doesn’t find something to focus on, he’s fucked’' and that 'If this teacher wasn’t there, I would not be having this conversation with you right now.'
claims.passage: "quite disruptive growing up," energy that "often" came out in "having fights," steadied by "really strong, protective and nurturing women," including a teacher he is still in contact with. "I wouldn’t have finished school without her," he said in 2022.
claims.inference: A reactive, combative early pattern that softened through protective allies fits a counterphobic Six reading; the lasting loyalty to the teacher fits Six's attachment to those who backed him. The same teacher credit recurs four years apart (2022, 2026), so it is a stable self-account, not a one-off.
claims.alternative: Fighting fits Eight; disruption fits Seven or his stated ADHD. This is the only source; do not build a childhood-wound causal story from it.

claims.claim: Square Mile reported in June 2022 (in the writer's narration) that he lives with ADHD; in that interview he said he is 'shit at focusing on something if I’m not interested in it' but gets 'obsessed' when he is, because 'it’s kind of a relief to be able to focus.'
claims.passage: shit at focusing on something if I’m not interested in it
claims.inference: The diagnosis is reported by the interviewer, not stated in a quoted sentence of his; the focus quotes are his own. Treated as context and as a confound for both 6 and 7, not as type evidence.
claims.alternative: Restless novelty-seeking might still be Seven independent of ADHD; the two are not mutually exclusive.

claims.claim: On Parade's End he told the director one of his lines was wrong ('I don’t know who the fuck I thought I was'); Benedict Cumberbatch, who 'said he’d had the same concern', then checked the book and found the line was right. He tells it to praise Cumberbatch as 'so studious'.
claims.passage: I don’t know who the fuck I thought I was
claims.inference: Challenging authority as a junior actor is a counterphobic move; his framing is self-deprecating, and the story's point for him is Cumberbatch's diligence.
claims.alternative: Eight-like assertiveness or One-like correctness; also a told-for-effect anecdote within a passage the writer flags as name-dropping.

claims.claim: He tore his ACL about six months before Clayface filming, put off surgery because he had booked the role, and, while telling the story unscripted on Empire's podcast, volunteered that 'for fear of losing this job, I didn't tell anybody' until a car-impact stunt forced him to take the stunt coordinator aside; Watkins confirms the team learned of it only then and that Harries still did the jump and fall.
claims.passage: And for fear of losing this job, I didn't tell anybody.
claims.inference: Shows a stated fear-of-loss motive. It does not discriminate Six from Three: losing a career-making lead threatens image as much as security, and any type might use the same phrase.
claims.alternative: Three: protecting the image of a capable, low-risk lead (he told THR he knew he was 'a potentially big risk for the studio', S26). Eight: toughness. Any first-time lead might hide an injury for career reasons; the motive word 'fear' is also ordinary speech. Earlier wording 'shot all of Clayface... hadn't told the stunts or anyone on production' (EW via S16) overstates the concealment; the podcast and Watkins place the disclosure mid-shoot.

claims.claim: Near the end of the Clayface shoot he pitched an unscripted club sequence to James Watkins; it was added and production extended filming by a day.
claims.passage: That was not in the script,
claims.inference: Creative initiative and play under exhaustion; the reported expectation of rejection hints at bracing for a no before asking.
claims.alternative: Seven-style spontaneity; the 'expected rejection' detail is the outlet's paraphrase of a video clip.

claims.claim: He repeatedly declines the star frame: 'I’m not a celebrity' (2020), most of Comic-Con 'would go, “Who?!”' (2026), and success is luck-heavy and 'isn’t a meritocracy' (2026).
claims.passage: the whole thing isn’t a meritocracy
claims.inference: Counts against Three: he volunteers rejection counts and luck instead of building an image of inevitability.
claims.alternative: British actor modesty is a strong press convention, and self-deprecation can itself be image management.

claims.claim: A 2022 interviewer observed that he was 'unshy about dropping huge names', and that after mentioning Benedict Cumberbatch 'He catches my eye to note my reaction.'
claims.passage: He catches my eye to note my reaction.
claims.inference: The interviewer's observation suggests attention to how he lands; the article labels 'monitoring how he lands' as an inference from Rudling's detail.
claims.alternative: A single journalist's reading of one glance; checking a listener's reaction also fits Six (reading the room) or ordinary storytelling.

claims.claim: Asked about vanity in Clayface, he said 'the vanity of it never interested me. I find it interesting because I feel like I have a relationship to it.'
claims.passage: I feel like I have a relationship to it.
claims.inference: An admitted personal relationship to appearance, in a job where his face is the product; relevant to the Three alternative but left unexplained by him.
claims.alternative: Physical prep and looks are part of his job; he immediately reframes it as craft ('part of my job').

claims.claim: He shows wide-ranging curiosity and side passions: he wants to study clowning in Paris, is described in 2022 as a keen pianist and guitarist, and said then that he has 'ridden bikes for years' (his bike 'conked out at the start of the pandemic').
claims.passage: go study clowning at Le Coq in Paris
claims.inference: The core of the Seven alternative: appetite for novelty and many open doors.
claims.alternative: Curiosity is common across types and in actors; he chooses motorbikes as 'an antidote' because of their mechanical certainty (C19), which points away from Seven.

claims.claim: He calls motorbikes 'an antidote' to acting ('I love doing manual stuff'; the writer has him 'tinkering with his motorbikes') because 'Acting is so subjective and sort of heady but there’s nothing subjective about whether an engine works or if a sprocket’s out of place.'
claims.passage: there’s nothing subjective about whether an engine works or if a sprocket’s out of place.
claims.inference: His relief is objective certainty, a Six (or Five/One) comfort, not novelty for its own sake.
claims.alternative: Simple hobby talk; many people like manual work as a break from screens.

claims.claim: In 2020 he called acting 'a pretty reckless choice of career', said he has been self-sufficient since 17, and said 'With optimism, I will always make decisions that I feel might come off.'
claims.passage: I chose to be an actor which on the surface seems to be a pretty reckless choice of career
claims.inference: Optimistic risk-taking is the Seven alternative's best self-report; for a Six it would be the counterphobic leap.
claims.alternative: He frames it while comparing himself to a hedonist character he plays, which invites a playful self-portrait.

claims.claim: In a 2026 conversation, Kit Connor said they 'could be silly' on their shoot together nine years earlier, which he had 'tried to carry forward and learn from you'; Harries replied, 'I may have taken the license to be silly and run with it,' and Connor then added, 'You taught me how to misbehave on a film set.'
claims.passage: I may have taken the license to be silly and run with it.
claims.inference: Playfulness on set supports Seven; it also shows the counterphobic Six's ease once he trusts the group.
claims.alternative: Banter between friends, not a behavioral record.

claims.claim: WalesOnline printed him saying he really pulled out his own tooth for a White Lines scene; weeks later he told Mr Porter he had been misquoted, 'I was doing a gag... It was just me not reading the room. But no, I didn’t pull my tooth out.'
claims.passage: I actually pulled it out! It’s real, that whole scene is real. I haven’t told anyone that.
claims.inference: A revealing, unflattering moment: a deadpan provocation printed as fact, then corrected with self-blame. Shows impulsive humor and concern for the record.
claims.alternative: The WalesOnline writer may have misread tone; it is his word against a printed quote. Present both, attributed and dated.

claims.claim: He leans on a fatalistic saying for peace: 'what is meant for you, won’t pass you by... everything happens for a reason and that gives me some kind of peace' (Glamour, 2020).
claims.passage: I really hold onto, ‘what is meant for you, won’t pass you by.’ I am not religious in particular
claims.inference: Equanimity language that fits Nine at least as well as Six; presented in the Nine section as rival evidence.
claims.alternative: Common show-business coping lines; written answers (S11) are composed.

claims.claim: In the Cultured Q&A conducted a couple of days before the 2026-10-23 release he said he does not know how to do anything else and has 'had way more noes than I’ve had yeses'; in 2020 he said he has 'countless more rejections than acceptances'.
claims.passage: I’ve had way more noes than I’ve had yeses,
claims.inference: Persistence through a long supporting-actor career (2011-2025) before a studio lead; durable behavior that fits Six's loyalty to a chosen path.
claims.alternative: Three persistence toward success; or Nine inertia ('I don’t know how to do anything else').

claims.claim: Watkins said at the premiere 'I don’t think I’ve ever auditioned anyone that much'; Harries said the process ran over three months with two long screen tests and 'I’m untested in this space, so I was glad he did it with me really because it meant that we’d had time to workshop the thing before he got onto set.'
claims.passage: I’m untested in this space, so I was glad he did it with me really because it meant that we’d had time to workshop the thing before he got onto set.
claims.inference: He welcomed extended testing as preparation and reassurance, matching C02, rather than resenting it as doubt about his talent.
claims.alternative: Diplomatic premiere talk about a director; relayed via A.V. Club from THR (not opened).

claims.claim: Tom Rhys Harries was born in Cardiff, Wales, in 1990 and is a first-language Welsh speaker.
claims.passage: born in Cardiff in 1990 and a first-language Welsh speaker
claims.inference: Biographical metadata. 1990 is supported by Wikipedia and by his own age references (26 in September 2017 per S02; 35 while filming in 2025 per S03).
claims.alternative: 2020-2022 press gave ages (27, 28, 29) that conflict with an October 1990 birth date; print the year only. The 8 October date is unverified in a primary. S04 says his 'mum used to be a writer', so describe her work cautiously. 2026 press still conflicts: THR said 'Now 36' on 2026-10-29 (S26), Nation.Cymru said 35 on 2026-10-27 (S29), and several film databases list 1992. Print 1990 as the year only, with no day.

claims.claim: He trained at the Royal Welsh College of Music & Drama, was cast in Hunky Dory (2011) while a student, kept studying, and graduated in 2012.
claims.passage: graduating in 2012
claims.inference: Chose to finish training after an early break, consistent with a preference for preparation.
claims.alternative: WWD (S10) says he 'soon left' the college after Hunky Dory; his own two accounts and Wikipedia's 2012 graduation outweigh it.

claims.claim: Before Clayface he worked for well over a decade, starting with Hunky Dory (2011) while a drama student, a lead role as Axel in Netflix's White Lines (2020), and on the West End stage including The Seagull opposite Emilia Clarke (shut after five performances in 2020, revived in 2022).
claims.passage: had been working for well over a decade before that
claims.inference: Career metadata showing a long stage-and-supporting record before the studio lead.
claims.alternative: Sources split on 2013 vs 2014 for the Mojo debut (production ran late 2013 into 2014); say 'opened in 2013' or 'in 2013-14'. THR (S26, 2026) also says 2014.

claims.claim: DC Studios cast him as Matt Hagen/Clayface in June 2025; the film opened in the US on October 23, 2026 at No. 1 with about $24 million (studio estimates).
claims.passage: The film opened at No. 1 in the US on October 23, 2026, with about [$24 million]
claims.inference: The current catalyst for search interest; context only, not type evidence.
claims.alternative: Opening figures are studio estimates and outlets differ ($43M global per Variety via S29; $46.5M global per THR S27); budget reports range from about $30M to $44M. Use rounded, dated figures or omit.
claims.review_trigger: Update with final domestic/worldwide gross, any sequel or DCU return announcement, and awards-season mentions; recheck by 2027-01-31.

claims.claim: Six days after the No. 1 opening he credited the people around him: grateful 'because you realize how many people have invested their time and work into this thing', said leading a big production is 'actually easier when you have so many people around you', and that 'fundamentally nothing is going to change — it might open a few more doors in terms of who I’m able to talk to', beyond wanting to work with 'creators who I back fundamentally.'
claims.passage: because you realize how many people have invested their time and work into this thing
claims.inference: One post-release interview, consistent with Six (credit placed in the network) but also with Nine steadiness and British press modesty; presented as a dated checkpoint, not a decisive test.
claims.alternative: Gratitude to crew is standard press etiquette, and British understatement is a convention. A Nine could also say 'nothing is going to change'. It is a single post-release interview.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck post-release and next-lead press (Clayface awards season, any DCU return, the 2026 indie's release) by 2027-03-31: does he reframe the win as earned arrival (3), chase the next adventure and call preparation a cage (7), or keep crediting the people around him (6)? Update the Who has his back and closing sections either way.

claims.claim: During the screen tests he told his agent 'Do not tell me who else it is' so he could stay 'in the zone', asked for the names only once 'it would no longer affect me negatively because I was done', and when called back for a second test said 'I had to put my blinders on.'
claims.passage: Do not tell me who else it is
claims.inference: He manages anticipatory pressure by controlling what information reaches him. That fits a Six managing anxiety, and it matches the Elden Ring and cycling distraction he described in the same period (C04).
claims.alternative: Three: avoiding comparison to protect performance. Nine: tuning out disturbance. Many actors use the same routine, so it is a craft habit as much as a motive.

claims.claim: He described himself as a risky bet for the studio: the other contenders had 'a proof of concept for leading a studio film', while with him 'there are so many moments where an unknown quality could falter... they haven’t got a great reference point as to what I’d be like with the crew, the rest of the cast, and in the press.'
claims.passage: there are so many moments where an unknown quality could falter
claims.inference: Spontaneously modelling the decision-maker's worst case and the points where he could fail is Six-style threat scanning. It also gives context to the injury concealment (C12).
claims.alternative: Three: worrying about how he is perceived, including 'in the press', is image concern. It may also be an accurate industry analysis rather than anxiety.

claims.claim: In unscripted audio he opens by turning the interview on the host (quizzing him about his golf handicap, 'I have my sources, Chris') and jokes 'I don't know. I rarely know what's going on.'
claims.passage: I have my sources, Chris
claims.inference: Playful deflection and banter support the Seven alternative (C21) and show a light public persona that the fear-and-preparation self-description does not predict.
claims.alternative: Deflecting with humour can also be a Six's way to ease tension at the start of a high-stakes press run (phobic charm), or simply junket fatigue. It is one Zoom interview.

claims.claim: On the Empire Film Podcast he recalled telling the stunt coordinator, 'Jimmy, I'm so sorry, man. I actually don't have an ACL.'
claims.passage: Jimmy, I'm so sorry, man. I actually don't have an ACL,
claims.inference: Pins the moment and manner of disclosure in his own unscripted words: an apology, at the point the stunt made concealment dangerous.
claims.alternative: Machine transcript (whisper small.en); punctuation and filler approximate. Told as a comic beat in a promotional podcast.

claims.claim: After tearing his ACL he booked Clayface and thought, 'Well, I’m not gonna have time to do the surgery.'
claims.passage: Well, I’m not gonna have time to do the surgery.
claims.inference: He chose the role over treatment, a costly choice that sets up the concealment.
claims.alternative: Scheduling realities of a studio shoot would push any actor the same way; not type-specific.

claims.claim: James Watkins told THR the injury came out during the car-hit stunt: 'There’s a moment in the film when Matt gets hit by a car, and that’s when it came out. Tom had a quiet word with the stunt man about it.'
claims.passage: There’s a moment in the film when Matt gets hit by a car, and that’s when it came out. Tom had a quiet word with the stunt man about it.
claims.inference: Independent corroboration from the director that disclosure happened mid-shoot and quietly, consistent with Harries's podcast account.
claims.alternative: Promo-cycle testimony from the director who cast him; not an independent intimate.

claims.claim: Watkins said Harries 'still did the jump and the fall, but he was frank about it', and the team finessed the stunt.
claims.passage: He still did the jump and the fall, but he was frank about it.
claims.inference: Shows physical risk-taking continued after disclosure, the counterphobic thread.
claims.alternative: Director's affectionate framing in a post-opening interview; also fits Eight toughness or Three image of capability.

claims.claim: In a July 2026 EW cover story, relayed by Instinct, he said 'I actually shot all of Clayface with a torn ACL. I hadn’t told the stunts or anyone on production.' His later podcast account and Watkins place the disclosure mid-shoot.
claims.passage: I actually shot all of Clayface with a torn ACL. I hadn’t told the stunts or anyone on production.
claims.inference: The earlier wording overstates the concealment relative to his own later account and Watkins's; the article presents both and prefers the later, corroborated version.
claims.alternative: The EW original (S17) could not be opened, so the wording rests on the Instinct relay (S16), which may compress the story. 'Shot all of it with a torn ACL' is true in that the ligament stayed torn; 'hadn't told anyone' conflicts only on timing.

claims.claim: DC Studios chose him in June 2025 from a reported shortlist that included Jack O'Connell, Tom Blyth and George MacKay.
claims.passage: ahead of a reported shortlist that included Jack O'Connell, Tom Blyth and George MacKay
claims.inference: Context for the stakes he describes and for his self-description as the riskier bet (C37).
claims.alternative: Trade reporting of a shortlist; casting lists are often incomplete.

claims.claim: The type answer: Type 6 at medium confidence, Type 7 closest rival, Type 3 also in play.
claims.passage: Tom Rhys Harries reads most clearly as an Enneagram Type 6, the security-seeking type, at medium confidence.
claims.inference: Summarizes the type hypothesis built from C01-C06, C12, C19, C26, C35-C37.
claims.alternative: Seven (C18, C20, C21, C38) and Three (C16, C17, C37) remain live; evidence is mostly promotional self-report.

claims.claim: In October 2026 he said of his school years, 'if this kid doesn’t find something to focus on, he’s fucked', and 'If this teacher wasn’t there, I would not be having this conversation with you right now.'
claims.passage: If this teacher wasn’t there, I would not be having this conversation with you right now.
claims.inference: The teacher credit recurs four years after S01, a stable self-account of loyalty to those who backed him.
claims.alternative: Post-release gratitude is expected in press; do not build a causal childhood story on it.

claims.claim: Watkins said at the premiere, 'I don’t think I’ve ever auditioned anyone that much.'
claims.passage: I don’t think I’ve ever auditioned anyone that much.

type_hypothesis.against: Most of the Six evidence is self-report in promotional settings, where actors routinely talk about nerves, trust and gratitude; his own gloss 'fear is a mark of caring' (C75) is common actor rhetoric. The fear he names in 2022 is fear of criticism (C01), which fits Three as well. Testimony comes from co-stars and the director in premiere season (C07, C26, C70), with nothing from long-term intimates (C62). Breadth of interests, optimism, playfulness, the club-scene improvisation, the gleeful 'get away with it' framing and the podcast banter (C13, C18, C20, C21, C38, C65) read Seven, and his screen-test escapes (C04, C49) are Seven-compatible anxiety avoidance. Name-dropping while watching the listener's reaction, hiding a torn ACL to keep a career-making role, awareness of how he would come across 'in the press', and an admitted 'relationship' to vanity (C12, C16, C17, C37) read Three; the ACL motive phrase does not separate 3 from 6. A calm, unhurried surface noted by interviewers, a thick skin, fatalist sayings and 'nothing is going to change' (C23, C35, C66, C67, C68, C69) read Nine. ADHD as reported by Square Mile (C10) confounds both the distractibility and the interest-driven focus. Counterphobic Six is not used to absorb the bold behavior. No wing or subtype is supported.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Seven: he wants to study clowning in Paris, plays guitar and rides motorbikes (C18); daydreamed Truman Show scenarios to make a paper round 'less mundane' (C54); calls acting a 'reckless' career he chose 'with optimism' (C20); 'took the license to be silly' and taught a teenage co-star to misbehave on set (C21); managed audition stress by escaping into Elden Ring and cycling (C04, C49), which is the classic Seven response to anxiety; described hiding the knee as 'trying to get away with it' (C65); pitched an unscripted club sequence (C13), and opened a 2026 podcast by interviewing the host about golf (C38). He also chose to go into a 2026 indie unprepared (C64). Three is a further live rival (C12, C16, C17, C37), and Nine fits the calm surface interviewers describe (C66-C69, C23).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: Narrow, and resting on a few statements rather than the escapes or the ACL phrase. Against Seven: he calls preparation a crutch he is used to leaning on and going in without it 'terrifying' (2026, C02), and the antidote to acting's subjectivity he describes most fondly is mechanical certainty, 'nothing subjective about whether an engine works' (2022, C19), not novelty. Both are single quotes, and he did choose to go in blind. Against Three: his anxiety attaches to preparing and performing rather than reception ('gone past the point of nervousness' a couple of days before release, C66), and he places credit in trusted collaborators across years (Pina 2020, C52; the people invested in Clayface 2026, C35) rather than in himself. Against Nine: he repeatedly names fear and anxiety (C01, C04, C78) and actively engineers preparation and information control (C02, C36) instead of downplaying disturbance. The fear-as-driver self-description dates to 2022, not 2015 (C78, C77).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Hiding the torn ACL until a stunt forced disclosure (C12) fits Six and Three equally; his stated motive 'for fear of losing this job' is ordinary speech, and by Watkins's account the feared loss would not have happened (C70). The printed-then-retracted tooth-pulling joke (C22), the podcast role-reversal banter (C38), the gleeful 'get away with it' framing (C65), challenging a director on Parade's End (C11) and the childhood fights (C09) show a provocative, playful streak that a cautious Six does not predict and that the article leaves partly unexplained rather than absorbing into counterphobic Six. His offhand entry into acting (C73) sits awkwardly with the vigilance reading. He admits a personal 'relationship' to vanity without explaining it (C17). Wing unknown (6w7 plausible, not argued).
